reviewLens: safety and harm: eating-disorder screening, minors, pregnancy, messaging
notes: Checked against primary sources fetched on 2026-11-17: NICE NG69 recommendations page, Morgan 1999 (PMC28290), Kutz 2020 (PMC7080881), IOC REDs 2023 consensus (bjsm.bmj.com/content/57/17/1073), Roberts 2020 (PMC7052702), Helms 2014 (PMC4033492), ACOG patient FAQ119 (the ACOG Committee Opinion 804 full text was paywalled and could not be read), CDC maternal diet page, WHO BMI-for-age 5-19 page, DGHS Tele MANAS page, NEDC Eating Disorder Safe Section 3 PDF. Confirmed correct and not reported as issues: SCOFF wording and scoring, NICE NG69 rec numbers 1.2.4/1.2.5/1.2.6, CDC +330-400 kcal for breastfeeding, Tele MANAS 14416 and 1800-89-14416 (same digits as the spec's 1-800-891-4416), and the WHO adult BMI cut-off of 18.5. The web-search budget ran out during this review, so sources were reached by direct URL or DOI only.

issues.problem: The params sensitivityPct=100 and specificityPct=87.5 come from the original validation study. That study tested only women aged 18-40: specialist-clinic cases with anorexia or bulimia, and college-recruited controls. No men were tested. A later meta-analysis found lower pooled accuracy and lower sensitivity in samples with more men (0.75 in mixed-sex samples vs 0.88 in majority-female samples). It also found lower sensitivity when binge eating disorder was included, and concluded there is not enough evidence to use SCOFF for the full range of DSM-5 eating disorders. Forge's user is a male lifter, so the 100% figure overstates how reliably a negative screen rules out a problem. Q4 also asks only about feeling 'fat when others say you are too thin', which does not capture drive for muscularity. Helms 2014 note that muscle dysmorphia is higher in male natural bodybuilders.
issues.correction: params: replace sensitivityPct 100 / specificityPct 87.5 with pooledSensitivity 0.86 (95% CI 0.78-0.91), pooledSpecificity 0.83 (95% CI 0.77-0.88), maleMixedSampleSensitivity 0.75, and keep the original figures only as originalStudyWomenOnly {sensitivityPct: 100, specificityPct: 87.5}. Rule text to add: 'A negative SCOFF never counts as clearance and never unlocks any feature. SCOFF was validated in women with anorexia/bulimia and is less sensitive in men and for binge eating disorder. Concerns raised outside SCOFF (free text, check-in answers, muscle-size preoccupation, post-cut binge episodes) route to the same help-seeking path as a positive screen.'
issues.source: Morgan, Reid & Lacey 1999, BMJ 319:1467, https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.319.7223.1467 (PMC28290); Kutz et al. 2020, J Gen Intern Med 35(3):885-893, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-019-05478-6 (PMC7080881); Helms, Aragon & Fitschen 2014, JISSN, https://doi.org/10.1186/1550-2783-11-20

issues.problem: No rule covers a user who discloses self-harm, suicidal thoughts, purging (vomiting), or misuse of laxatives, diet pills or diuretics in free text to the LLM coach or in notes. NICE NG69 says people with a suspected eating disorder should be assessed for self-harm and suicide risk, and for the need for emergency care. Tele MANAS already appears in the spec but is only reached through a positive SCOFF.
issues.correction: Add rule safety_crisis_disclosure: appliesWhen = any free text (coach chat, notes, check-ins) is classified as self-harm/suicidal ideation, purging, or laxative/diet-pill/diuretic misuse. action = stop all coaching output for that turn; do not give nutrition or training advice; show a crisis card with tap-to-call Tele MANAS 14416 (toll-free 1800-89-14416, 24x7) and 112 for immediate danger; apply the same locks as safety_scoff_positive_response (maintenance, weight-loss and photo body-fat features paused); never quote or score the user's words back to them. params: {teleManasShortCode: 14416, teleManasTollFree: '1800-89-14416', emergencyNumber: 112}.
issues.source: NICE NG69 (2017, updated 2020) recs 1.2.6 and 1.2.9, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng69/chapter/Recommendations; DGHS MoHFW National Mental Health Programme page (Tele MANAS: 'toll-free helpline number 1800-89-14416 or short code 14416', 24x7), https://dghs.mohfw.gov.in/national-mental-health-programme.php

issues.problem: The check-in triggers only on intake below the floor, rapid weight loss, or attempts to set a target below the floor. NICE NG69 rec 1.2.6 also lists compensatory behaviours (laxative or diet-pill misuse, vomiting, excessive exercise), menstrual or other endocrine disturbances, and physical signs (dizziness, palpitations, fainting) as reasons to consider assessment. The IOC REDs consensus defines disordered eating to include excessive exercise beyond assigned training to make up for food eaten. For males it names low libido and fewer morning erections as emerging REDs indicators. An app that logs both cardio and food can see some of these patterns, but no rule uses them.
issues.correction: Add triggers to the rule and params: (d) unplanned cardio/extra sessions logged on >= 3 of 7 days while in a deficit, or the user explains extra exercise as making up for food ('burn off', 'earn'); (e) user reports vomiting, laxative, diet-pill or diuretic use, which routes to safety_crisis_disclosure; (f) female users report missed or stopped periods; male users report low libido or reduced morning erections during a deficit; (g) user reports dizziness, palpitations or fainting while in a deficit, which also fires safety_medical_red_flags_stop. params additions: {unplannedCardioDaysIn7: 3}; the threshold of 3 is an app convention.
issues.source: NICE NG69 rec 1.2.6, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng69/chapter/Recommendations; Mountjoy et al. 2023 IOC REDs consensus, Br J Sports Med 57:1073, https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994

issues.problem: The block applies only once BMI is already < 18.5. It does not stop a user at, say, BMI 19 from saving a goal weight below BMI 18.5 or a cut whose projected end weight crosses it. NICE NG69 gives 'dieting when they are underweight' as a reason to consider assessment. The rule also applies the adult cut-off to everyone, but for 5-19-year-olds WHO defines thinness by BMI-for-age (< -2 SD), not by 18.5.
issues.correction: Rule addition: 'Forge refuses any goal weight, and any cut whose projected end weight at the planned rate, that implies BMI < 18.5 (adults). A refused low goal counts as one belowFloorAttempt for safety_low_intake_rapid_loss_checkin. For users under 18 (and 18-19 if age is known), use WHO BMI-for-age: thinness = < -2 SD, severe thinness = < -3 SD; never show adult BMI categories to minors.' params additions: {blockGoalWeightBelowBmi: 18.5, minorThinnessZ: -2, minorSevereThinnessZ: -3}.
issues.source: NICE NG69 recs 1.2.6-1.2.7, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng69/chapter/Recommendations; WHO Growth reference 5-19 years, BMI-for-age (Thinness < -2SD; Severe thinness < -3SD), https://www.who.int/tools/growth-reference-data-for-5to19-years/indicators/bmi-for-age

issues.problem: Only photo body-fat estimation and body-fat goals are disabled. Body-fat values from BIA, skinfolds or the 'body-fat estimate x bodyweight' path used by the energy-availability rule stay active, and the rule says nothing about BMI display. The IOC REDs consensus says body-composition assessment is recommended only for medical purposes under 18 years, with guardian consent and team agreement in exceptional cases. Its framework treats height, weight, anthropometrics and skinfolds as body-composition assessments.
issues.correction: action: 'If age < 18: disable entry, estimation and display of body-fat % from any method (photo, BIA, skinfold, formula); do not compute FFM-based energy availability from estimated body fat; do not display BMI categories (use WHO BMI-for-age only, inside safety checks, not shown as a label); bodyweight logging is optional and off by default, with no trend chart against a target. Body-composition values from a clinician may be stored but not used to set goals.' params additions: {minAgeForAnyBodyFatEstimate: 18}.
issues.source: Mountjoy et al. 2023 IOC REDs consensus, section 'Body composition assessment and management' ('body composition assessment is recommended only for medical purposes under 18 years of age'), https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994; WHO BMI-for-age 5-19 years, https://www.who.int/tools/growth-reference-data-for-5to19-years/indicators/bmi-for-age

issues.problem: The spec says its warning-sign list was not checked. ACOG's patient guidance lists 9 signs to stop exercise; the rule omits 'muscle weakness', and the userMessage names only 5 of the 9. The rule also leaves out ACOG precautions that matter for a lifting program: avoid lying flat on the back or standing still for long periods, avoid overheating (including hot yoga/Pilates), and avoid fall-risk and contact activities, scuba diving and exertion above 6,000 ft unless already living at altitude. ACOG also advises discussing exercise with an ob-gyn at early prenatal visits, and says that if weight starts to fall, calories may need to rise. The forced 'Congratulations' opener assumes how the user feels about the pregnancy.
issues.correction: Rule warning-sign list (stop and call obstetric provider): vaginal bleeding; feeling dizzy or faint; shortness of breath before starting exercise; chest pain; headache; muscle weakness; calf pain or swelling; regular painful uterine contractions; fluid gushing or leaking from the vagina. Add to action: 'Swap prolonged supine exercises (e.g. flat bench, lying leg raises) for incline or seated variants and avoid long motionless standing; no hot-room sessions; flag fall-risk and contact activities; keep the deficit block and alert if the 7-day average weight falls.' userMessage: 'During pregnancy Forge won't set a calorie deficit or weight-loss goal. Please check your training plan with your doctor or midwife, and stop and call them if you have bleeding, dizziness or faintness, chest pain, headache, muscle weakness, calf pain or swelling, painful contractions, leaking fluid, or breathlessness before exercise.'
issues.source: ACOG FAQ119 'Exercise During Pregnancy' (updated Sept 2024, reviewed Nov 2025), https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/exercise-during-pregnancy; ACOG Committee Opinion 804 (2020, reaffirmed 2023), https://doi.org/10.1097/AOG.0000000000003772 (full text paywalled, not re-read)

issues.problem: The photo body-fat feature is enabled for any adult who has not had a positive SCOFF in the last 30 days, which includes users who have never been screened. The IOC REDs consensus says body-composition assessment should include prescreening for body-image concerns and problematic eating behaviours. Roberts 2020 recommend scheduled, supervised physique assessment rather than frequent physique checking. They note cross-sectional links between self-monitoring and shape checking and binge eating and shape/weight overvaluation.
issues.correction: action: 'Before first use, and before any estimate if the last screen is more than 12 weeks old, require a completed SCOFF plus the low-intake check-in questions; block if positive or if any safety_crisis_disclosure / safety_low_intake_rapid_loss_checkin event is open. Keep the 14-day minimum between estimates.' params additions: {requireScreenWithinWeeks: 12}; the 12-week value is an app convention matching rescreenEveryWeeksDuringCut.
issues.source: Mountjoy et al. 2023 IOC REDs consensus ('This should include prescreening to assess body image concerns and problematic eating behaviours'), https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994; Roberts et al. 2020, J Hum Kinet 71:79-108, https://doi.org/10.2478/hukin-2019-0096 (PMC7052702)

issues.problem: The low-body-fat block and caution use the photo point estimate. The spec itself says the estimate is unvalidated and can be off by about 5 percentage points. Using the point estimate is not the conservative direction: if a true 7% is read as 12%, the user passes the < 8% block and gets only a caution. The IOC REDs consensus says 'doubly indirect' methods that rely on regression equations, such as consumer BIA, do not give valid data and are strongly affected by hydration. Yet the rule accepts BIA on the same footing as DXA and skinfolds.
issues.correction: photo_bf_accuracy_limits rule text: replace 'the low-body-fat block uses the point estimate' with 'safety blocks and cautions use the LOWER bound of the displayed range (point estimate - displayRangeHalfWidthPctPoints)'. safety_low_body_fat_no_deficit appliesWhen: 'for photo and BIA estimates, compare thresholds against estimate - 5 percentage points; for DXA or multi-site skinfolds by a trained operator, use the reported value'. params addition: {lowConfidenceMethodSafetyOffsetPctPoints: 5}.
issues.source: Mountjoy et al. 2023 IOC REDs consensus, section 'Body composition assessment and management' (doubly indirect methods 'do not provide valid data'; skinfolds, DXA and B-mode ultrasound proposed), https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994

issues.problem: The userMessage states as fact that intake below 30 kcal/kg FFM 'can affect hormones, recovery, bones and mood'. The IOC 2023 consensus says a universal 30 kcal/kg FFM/day cut-off is debated even in females, and that the threshold for males is less understood but appears lower (about 9-25 kcal/kg FFM/day). With FFM taken from rough photo or BIA body-fat values, a hard 30 line for a male user will often fire falsely and turns an uncertain estimate into a health claim. The IOC uses symptoms and signs (via CAT2), not EA alone.
issues.correction: Keep eaWarnKcalPerKgFfm 30 as a conservative prompt, but change the rule text to: 'EA < 30 is a prompt to check in, not evidence of harm; the threshold is debated in females and appears lower in males (IOC 2023). FFM from photo/BIA estimates is low-confidence.' userMessage: 'Your planned intake may be low for the amount you train. If you've noticed low energy, poor sleep, low libido, missed periods or stalled lifts, Forge suggests nudging today's target up to about {suggestedKcal} kcal.' Pair the warning with the symptom questions in safety_low_intake_rapid_loss_checkin.
issues.source: Mountjoy et al. 2023 IOC REDs consensus, sections on LEA in males ('a universal cut-off of 30 kcal/kg FFM/day ... is debated'; males 'appears to be lower (eg, ~9 to 25 kcal/kg FFM/day)'; low libido and decreased morning erections as emerging male indicators), https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994

issues.problem: The lock wording 'For at least 30 days, or until the user confirms a professional has reviewed them' is ambiguous. Read as 'whichever comes first', one self-attestation tap lifts every lock straight away. The help-seeking advice names only 'a GP or psychiatrist'. NICE says a suspected eating disorder should be referred to an eating-disorder service. Helms 2014 recommend early intervention by specialists experienced in both bodybuilding and eating disorders.
issues.correction: Rule text: 'Locks last a minimum of 30 days. Confirming a professional review does not shorten the minimum; after 30 days the lock lifts only after a re-offered SCOFF is negative and no safety_crisis_disclosure or low-intake event is open.' userMessage help line: 'You can talk to your doctor and ask about an eating-disorder specialist (ideally one who works with athletes or lifters), or call Tele MANAS free at 14416 any time.'
issues.source: NICE NG69 recs 1.2.5 and 1.2.10, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng69/chapter/Recommendations; Helms, Aragon & Fitschen 2014, JISSN ('Early therapeutic intervention by specialists with experience in competitive bodybuilding and eating disorders'), https://doi.org/10.1186/1550-2783-11-20 (PMC4033492)

issues.problem: No rule controls how bodyweight is shown. If raw daily weigh-ins are displayed by default, every daily fluctuation feeds the self-weighing and checking behaviours that Roberts 2020 tie to distress in physique athletes. Their harm-mitigation table recommends using bodyweight averages and ranges instead.
issues.correction: Add to action: 'Weight screens show the 7-day moving average and weekly change by default; raw daily weigh-ins are behind a tap and never notified. Calorie targets are displayed as a range (target +/- 100 kcal) rather than a single number.' The +/-100 kcal width is an app convention.
issues.source: Roberts et al. 2020, J Hum Kinet, Table 1 'Hypothetical seasonal guidelines for mitigating harm in physique sport' (e.g. 'Macronutrient or calorie ranges versus food source restriction'; 'Scheduled, supervised physique assessment, body weight averages'), https://doi.org/10.2478/hukin-2019-0096 (PMC7052702)

issues.problem: Two sample messages work against the spec's own messaging rules. The diet-break message leads with weight lost ('You've lost {kg} kg so far'). The photo sample praises visible change in shoulder and back muscle ('Nice training progress'), which is still praise for appearance. NEDC's communicator guidance advises moving health content away from weight loss and using language that focuses on physical and mental health and wellbeing rather than appearance. Also, the NEDC Section 3 document cited across the spec is written for media and communicators. It states that its harm-minimisation principles for people already unwell are not directly applicable to that setting, so it should not be the only support for one-to-one coaching copy.
issues.correction: nutrition_diet_breaks userMessage: 'You've been in a deficit for {weeks} weeks. This is a good time for a week at maintenance. It doesn't undo your progress, and it often makes the next stretch easier.' photo_no_attractiveness_commentary userMessage: 'Compared with 8 weeks ago, the estimated body-fat range is similar. Your logged lifts are up over the same period.' (Performance praise only; no body-part appearance praise.) Add Roberts 2020 and NICE NG69 next to the NEDC citation in the safety_messaging_* rules.
issues.source: National Eating Disorders Collaboration, Eating Disorder Safe principles, Section 3 (communicators, media and relevant platforms), https://gatewayhealth.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Eating-Disorder-Safe-Principles_Section-3_Comms-Media-Platforms.pdf; Roberts et al. 2020, https://doi.org/10.2478/hukin-2019-0096
